To address this research gap, we draw on photo elicitation mappings of 101 journalistic and journalism-like actors in Austria and relate them to their position in the journalistic field. The findings show that both the core and the periphery are more nuanced, yet there are commonalities in their relational position-taking, which adds to our understanding of the journalistic field’s changing boundaries.

latest.title: Mapping Gaps in Local News Coverage
latest.abstract: Building on Anderson’s concept of imagined communities and Ball-Rokeach’s work on Communication Infrastructure Theory, we demonstrate how cartographic mapping can be used to help communities understand how the media construct their geographic area. We compare media coverage to other datasets about particular geographies, documenting gaps between the two. We do this work through four case studies. Each case study illustrates a unique way in which external data can be compared to coverage. We compare media coverage of Philadelphia locations to how many people live in various regions, the issues emphasized in the media and those that Philadelphia residents say are important for their neighborhoods, media coverage of crime that mentions various locations to crime statistics in Chicago, and data about the number of COVID cases in different parts of Chicago to news organizations’ Facebook posts about the disease. The gaps revealed by these analyses, we propose, allow for reflection on whether media coverage is serving the needs of communities. We conclude by discussing lessons learned about using mapping across these projects, and how similar studies can be used by communities and newsrooms.

latest.title: Moral Archivists and Agents of Accountability: Typologies of Advocacy Journalism in Local Indonesian Media's Coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy
latest.abstract: This study examines how local media implemented advocacy journalism in their coverage of the Kanjuruhan Tragedy, an event that killed 135 people and triggered prolonged collective trauma in Malang, Indonesia. Using a qualitative approach, the study analyzed 160 news articles and conducted in-depth interviews with journalists and editors from four local media outlets. The findings identify six typologies of advocacy journalism that are not isolated but interconnected, forming a dynamic spectrum of practices. Segmented Advocacy emerges as the dominant form through the direct representation of victims’ voices, often integrated with Emotional Advocacy to build public empathy. Meanwhile, Woven Advocacy and Counter-Frame Advocacy demonstrate strategic critiques that range from implicit to explicit challenges to state narratives. Emerging new typologies and Community Alliance further indicate the expansion of advocacy into cultural, spiritual, and collaborative engagement with civil society. The findings also reveal that institutional pressures and journalist polarization dynamics shape advocacy practices. These findings offer an empirically grounded perspective on advocacy journalism in the Global South, where local media act as moral archivists and agents of accountability sustaining collective memory and justice.

latest.title: “They Don’t Understand What it Means to be Poor”: How Representation, Relevance, and Relatability Shape the News Experience of Marginalised Young Adults
latest.abstract: There are significant concerns about young adults from low socioeconomic backgrounds becoming disengaged from the news. Drawing on 25 semi-structured interviews with participants aged 18–25 in England, this study examines how social inequality shapes how young adults experience news. Interviewees avoid legacy news media, citing a lack of representation, as stories about them and their communities are omitted from coverage. Where relevant topics are included, they feel that the reporting masks the complexity of how an issue impacts marginalised communities. Crucially, however, this group are not consistent news avoiders but remains engaged with news found on social platforms, accessing perspectives that resonate with their lived experience. This often comes from non-traditional actors who draw on new forms of journalistic storytelling. This paper argues that relatability—understood as a felt sense of proximity to news based on shared communicative norms, cultural experiences, and perceived social relevance—is crucial to understanding this population's news experience. By analysing relatability alongside representation and relevance, the study demonstrates how the interviewees’ lived experience of inequality shapes their relationship to news, both in its content and form. The paper offers practical recommendations for how inclusive storytelling and support for creator journalists can better serve this population.

latest.title: Perceiving the News as Toxic: A Longitudinal, Cross-National Analysis of Negative News Evaluations in Flanders and Ireland
latest.abstract: In today’s media environment, where information overload, negativity, and news fatigue are increasingly common, news can feel toxic. Yet little research examines how users perceive this toxicity and adjust their news practices in response. This study addresses that gap through a repeated cross-sectional analysis of Flanders and Ireland. Drawing on DNR-data from 2017-2025 and latent class analysis, we identify three archetypal news repertoires: Panoramic, Limited, and Traditional. Our findings reveal a shift toward limited repertoires, particularly among younger and less socioeconomically advantaged groups, while panoramic repertoires have become rarer, and traditional repertoires have remained stable. These shifts are associated with negative news attitudes, including distrust, avoidance, disinterest, fake news concerns and perceived fake news exposure. The cross-national comparison highlights sharper transitions in Flanders, whereas Irish users retained higher engagement, though early disengagement emerged. By linking negative attitudes or evaluations with changes in repertoires, we contribute to audience research and underscore the need to reconsider the journalism-audience relationship as disengagement is no longer marginal but increasingly mainstream. From a user perspective, repertoire narrowing may be understood as a coping response, although it risks deepening informational inequalities.

latest.title: Algorithmic News Selection Under News Avoidance: Assessing News Values on Chinese Tiktok (Douyin)
latest.abstract: This study explores how recommendation algorithms on Douyin respond to users’ growing disengagement from news by shaping the visibility of news content. Adopting an agent-based testing (ABT) approach, we conducted a 2 (intentional news avoidance: 0% vs. 100%) × 2 (unintentional news avoidance: 50% vs. 100%) between-subject experiment to simulate distinct user behaviors and capture large-scale data from news-related videos. Findings indicated that two avoidance behavioral patterns result in contrasting algorithmic outcomes which reinforce or weaken certain news values such as prominence, uniqueness, timeliness, and influence. A significant interaction effect further reveals that the influence of intentional news avoidance on the news values of influence diminishes as users’ preference for non-news content increases, whereas its influence on uniqueness becomes stronger. These findings show that recommender systems adapt to user disengagement by reprioritizing content, highlighting algorithmic curation as a socio-technical process that shapes attention amid selective news exposure.

latest.title: Soft Power from the Outside, Career Choice from the Inside: Understanding Job Attractions of Chinese Media Expats in Thailand
latest.abstract: China’s global media expansion is often interpreted as a state-led soft power strategy. Yet little is known about how individual journalists enact this expansion while working overseas for Chinese media organizations. Taking Thailand as an empirical case, this article examines how Chinese journalists assigned to overseas postings come to view their roles as a worthwhile career decision. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Thailand and in-depth interviews with Chinese expat journalists, it argues that alignment with state goals emerges not from ideological commitment, but from personal motivations, career timing, and everyday practical reasoning. The article draws on Bourdieu’s concept of illusio to conceptualize this process as a socially grounded belief that the pursuit is worth investment. Journalists accept overseas postings insofar as these roles make sense within their own trajectories, at once professionally viable and personally meaningful. The findings complement state-centric models of media expansion and offers a framework for understanding journalists’ on-the-ground motivations amid broader transformations in global journalism.

latest.title: The Many Notions of Audience Engagement: A Scoping Review
latest.abstract: In recent years, “audience engagement” and “engaged journalism” have emerged as buzzwords in journalism studies. Audience engagement is regularly discussed as a potential remedy for declining trust in journalism and its precarious financial situation. Over the past two decades, journalism studies have thus extensively analyzed the concept, resulting in a vast body of literature on engagement. However, this has created definitional confusion around audience engagement, with numerous definitions, interpretations and characteristics of the concept discussed in existing scholarship. By conducting a systematic scoping review of 174 peer-reviewed journal articles on audience engagement, this study sheds closer light on the existing research on engagement, offers an overview on theoretical and empirical conceptualizations, and examines goals and challenges associated with engagement. The review highlights how audience engagement is examined and conceptualized in journalism scholarship, and identifies key directions for future research.

latest.title: Black Lives Matter on the Ballot, in the Press: An Argument for Reporting the Long View of Contentious Solutions in Local Journalism
latest.abstract: This paper investigates how local journalists in Austin, Texas reported on a 2021 ballot initiative mandating increased police staffing. Representing a backlash to 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, the initiative followed efforts to reallocate funds away from the Austin Police Department. Grounded in interviews with journalists who described their news choices and positionality in relation to the initiative, this case study reveals how contentious solutions to intractable social problems exacerbate tensions inherent to dominant journalistic norms. Journalists adhering to impartiality described the initiative’s underlying conflict narrowly to avoid the appearance of bias; more alarmingly, some acted as unfiltered conduits for false information by viewing coverage as a public forum for debate. We evaluate these findings against solutions-oriented journalism—an umbrella term for emerging paradigms that prioritize constructive reporting on solutions to engage news audiences in civic life—and demonstrate how these models fall short when solutions themselves are sites of intense social struggle. Inspired by journalists who resisted norms of impartiality and balance to investigate histories and trajectories of local social action, we encourage proponents of solutions-oriented journalism to prioritize rigorous, factual reporting of the long view for audiences to engage with solutions as people continuously struggle to enact them.

latest.title: Journalistic Routines and the Social Construction of Race: A Critical Discourse Analysis of the Tyreek Hill Police Encounter
latest.abstract: To gauge U.S. journalism’s post-2020 racial reckoning, this article examines news coverage of football player Tyreek Hill’s police encounter in September 2024. Using Critical Discourse Analysis to interpret and explain digital media texts, this project mimics the contingency of the internet and considers local, national, legacy, digital-only, and sports outlets. Overall, it finds that news discourse continues to operate through a white racial frame. Even outlets that acknowledged systemic inequities or foregrounded the perspectives of the racially marginalized could recreate this dominant perspective, reinforcing tropes such as Black criminality, victim blaming, and deference to official sources. It’s thus argued that routine journalistic practices such as descriptive reporting, bothsidesism, headline conventions, reliance on official sources, and other supposedly objective norms, actually limit social discourse and the ability to have honest, good faith conversations about race. The project further highlights coverage that did counter the white racial frame and ultimately argues such coverage should be the standard. These practices are more ethical (i.e., take responsibility for the social consequences of news narratives) and provide a more nuanced and rigorous approximation of truth.

latest.title: Negotiating Professional Roles in a Constrained Media System: Role Perception and Narrated Enactment among Fact-Checkers in China
latest.abstract: This study offers the first detailed investigation into how Chinese fact-checkers perceive and narrate the enactment of professional roles within a constrained media environment. Drawing on 14 in-depth, semi-structured interviews with fact-checkers from four types of Chinese fact-checking organizations, the article provides rare qualitative evidence on a professional community that remains difficult to access. The study identifies six roles rooted in the Chinese media context: educator, rumor-buster, curator, independent advocate, gate-watcher, and facilitator. These roles show how fact-checkers negotiate professional ideals, institutional constraints, and national communication priorities in their everyday work. The article contributes to journalistic role theory by linking role perception with narrated role enactment. It shows that professional roles in constrained media systems are not simply adopted or abandoned, but situationally interpreted, negotiated, and combined. Rather than revealing a sharp divide between ideals and practice, the findings suggest a relatively strong convergence between perceived roles and narrated enactment. This convergence reflects the stability of Chinese fact-checkers’ professional self-image under institutional constraint. The article therefore demonstrates how Chinese fact-checkers articulate, justify, and normalize their professional roles, while foregrounding the symbolic and discursive processes through which perception and enactment are connected.

latest.title: Toward a Comprehensive Understanding of Journalists’ Emotional Well-Being: Precarity, Identity and Shared Concern in Latin America
latest.abstract: This study examines determinants of journalists’ emotional well-being. Drawing on stress and coping theory, role theory, and research on precarity and safety, it proposes a framework to explain concern about emotional well-being under workplace stress. Data come from the Worlds of Journalism Study in 10 Latin American countries with varying levels of press freedom. The dependent variable is a single-item report of concern about emotional well-being due to work. Hypotheses address gender, precarity, professional roles, victimization, coping, support, and press freedom. Findings show widespread concern driven by structural, organizational, and identity-based vulnerabilities. Indicators of precarity are the strongest predictors: heavier workloads increase concern, while higher income serves as a protective factor. Identity-related factors also matter: identifying as a woman and experiencing workplace bullying—reported more frequently by women—predict higher concern. Role discordance, or tension between self-censorship and professional values, further elevates concern. Unexpectedly, receiving colleague support after attacks is associated with greater concern, suggesting reactive coping or emotional contagion. Press freedom is not a significant predictor. Potential limitations include the single-item outcome and sensitivity of press freedom measures to local conditions. The study calls for organizational interventions while noting that addressing precarity requires structural changes to journalism’s financial model.

latest.title: Revisiting the Indian Emergency: Collective Memory and Political Narratives in English-language Dailies
latest.abstract: Although the press is credited with writing the first draft of history, the relevance of the past to journalists as “purveyors of the present” remains less understood, particularly in the Global South. This article grapples with this problem by investigating the uses of the past to journalism. Building on scholarship from journalism and memory studies, I investigate the contemporary news media’s references to the Indian Emergency (1975–1977), in which the government instituted strict controls on freedom of speech and the press. Specifically, by drawing on the concept of “collective memory,” I analyze how mainstream English-language dailies constructed narratives about the Emergency during April-June 2024, a period encompassing the 2024 national election and the anniversary of the Emergency. Narrative analysis reveals two themes in coverage. First, narratives harked back to the Emergency to highlight the ruling government’s suppression of the press in contemporary India. Second, narratives projected the Emergency as a site where political debates and differences between the ruling and opposition parties were played out. This article argues that the narrative use of vernacular linguistic registers, particularly in English-language newswriting, constitutes an important feature of collective memory work and journalistic invocation of the past in this Global South context.

latest.title: Reasserting the Relevance of Media Trust: A Response to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt (2023)
latest.abstract: This article responds to Jakobsson and Stiernstedt's (2023. “Trust and the media: Arguments for the (irr)elevance of a concept.” Journalism Studies 24 (4): 479–495) invitation to critically examine the significance of media trust. They argue that there “is a lack of strong arguments for why falling levels of trust in the news media are legitimately described as a crisis or problem” (479). Their critique offers a valuable counterpoint to the (often implicit) assumption that news media trust is always positive. Still, I argue for closer examination of their central arguments to move toward a comprehensive synthesis. I draw on political science literature and research on the consequences of media trust to reassert the importance of media trust for news consumption, democracy and ontological security. Without a comprehensive synthesis, debate over media trust risks becoming polarized and binary, with scholars selectively citing research that supports their views. The paperproposes two ways forward. First, a dynamic conceptualization of media trust similar to a “thermostat” where media trust provides a baseline openness to information, while vigilance operates as an adaptive regulator, selectively heightening scrutiny. Second, combining cultural and institutional perspectives to develop a more nuanced understanding of the significance of media trust.

latest.title: Between Watchdogs and Disseminators of Facts: Exploring How Spanish Journalists and Fact-checkers Perceive Their Roles Amidst Disinformation
latest.abstract: Although journalists and fact-checkers are expected to flag disinformation and point news users to trustworthy content, we know little about whether they feel empowered to fulfil these expectations. Building upon previous research on journalistic role perceptions in the context of disinformation, this study investigates how Spanish journalists and fact-checkers perceive their roles. The analysis of in-depth semi-structured interviews with 18 journalists and fact-checkers reveals that these professionals strongly advocate for their role as disseminators, interpreters, and watchdogs, emphasizing their unique commitment to delivering reliable information to empower citizens. However, a significant disparity exists between the two groups. While fact-checkers are dedicated to actively fighting disinformation and promote media literacy, journalists in mainstream media face difficulties in fulfilling basic journalistic functions due to the competitive media landscape and high pressure to increase revenue, compounded by the fragile economic structures of their organizations. As a major implication for journalism practice, this study shows that although media practitioners are willing to engage in fact-checking, there needs to be more support and awareness about their roles as watchdogs of truth.

latest.title: Towards an Adaptive Turn in Journalism: Conceptualizing the Algorithmic Co-Constitution of the News Media–Audience Relationship
latest.abstract: In this article, we introduce the term “adaptive turn” in the field of journalism to encapsulate the shift brought about by the introduction of algorithmic systems, such as predictive audience analytics, recommender systems, and generative AI technologies, across the news media industries. These algorithmic systems enable real-time adaptation to users’ individualized needs and actions based on their previous news consumption patterns. Previous literature and theorizing have dealt with either algorithmic systems focusing on the impact on journalistic values or practices or on the users’ algorithmic experiences, while our aim with the introduction of “the adaptive turn” is to conceptualize how these developments transform the relationship between the two separate fields. Building on an STS theoretical framework of technologies as mediating between humans and the world, we argue that the adaptive turn captures this shift to what we term the algorithmic co-constitution of the media/user relationship. By analysing current examples from existing literature, this paper pinpoints how this algorithmic co-constitution happens along four dimensions, namely a material, a normative, a commercial, and an epistemic dimension. Building on this, we suggest four research commitments going forward, which can qualify the identification of the social implications of the adaptive turn in journalism.

latest.title: Exploring Geographic “Reach” in Local Visual News: A Mapping Approach
latest.abstract: The importance of local news outlets having a physical presence in and understanding of the geographic places they serve is widely established in academic literature. Yet vast and sparsely populated coverage areas—such as those in regional, rural, or remote Australia—can challenge the feasibility and practicality of this ideal. This study explores the use of mapping methods to visualise and assess geographic patterns of visual news coverage published by two news outlets in communities in two different states, focusing on photographs as spatially anchored indicators of journalistic presence and attention. Specifically, we identify the locations of 701 news photographs published across the two outlets over a constructed year and then plot these on maps using a point-based approach. We then experiment with different ways of mapping these locations and reflect on the challenges of these approaches. In doing so, we highlight the value of using heat maps to more clearly reveal disparities in coverage density across the outlets’ self-defined “news zones”. Our findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of mapping approaches in identifying under-served areas and in complicating the issue of a news outlet’s “geographic” reach in the digital era.

latest.title: Local in Name Only? The Impact of Ownership and Newsroom Proximity on Local and Original News Coverage
latest.abstract: Local news plays a crucial democratic role by representing communities and reporting on place-based issues. Yet structural shifts such as chain ownership and the consolidation of local newsrooms risk diluting this local focus and increasing reliance on duplicated content. This study presents the first national analysis of local news authenticity in the UK using 465,105 articles from 360 outlets (2020–2022). We operationalise authentic localness using measures of geographic fidelity, coverage distance, and content duplication, and model how these vary by ownership and newsroom proximity. Our results show that corporate ownership reduces geographic fidelity and content originality, while increasing coverage distance, and that newsroom distance compounds this. Our findings demonstrate that ownership consolidation and newsroom centralisation jointly disembed journalism from communities, transforming local news from place-based reporting into networked content production.

latest.title: How Constructive is Constructive Journalism? Investigating Balance, Matter-of-Factness, and Focus on Solutions in German Constructive vs. Traditional News Media
latest.abstract: Constructive journalism is often viewed as a promising innovation for both journalism and democracy, yet it is also met with skepticism for being overly positive or advocative. While prior research has mainly examined its effects on the audience, little is known about how constructively oriented media actually report – especially compared to traditional news outlets. This study addresses this gap through a quantitative content analysis of about 2,000 news stories from four constructive and four comparable traditional German news media. Our findings first confirm constructive journalism as a three-dimensional concept including balance, matter-of-factness, and focus on solutions. Second, comparing constructive and traditional news outlets, we find that constructive media report in a considerably more solution-oriented manner, but significantly less balanced, reflecting a welfare-state-oriented and liberal-progressive stance. Finally, both display largely comparable levels of factual reporting. Thus, constructive media appear factual and solution-oriented but not balanced. However, as constructive journalism usefully complements traditional journalism by offering solutions and discussing future developments, we argue that strengthening solution-oriented reporting within traditional journalism may be more promising than establishing a pure constructive journalism model.

latest.title: Journalists Making an Exit: A Typology
latest.abstract: This study examines journalists leaving the profession against the backdrop of an increasingly precarious and unattractive career landscape in journalism; it focuses on the reasons for leaving, the exit pathways, and the individual-level consequences that follow this decision. Drawing on 38 qualitative interviews with former journalists in Germany, the study develops a five-part typology of journalism leavers based on established labor concepts. The Frustrated are experienced journalists who have become discontented with their work, whereas the Disillusioned are young journalists who decide to leave early in their careers. The Exhausted represent those who have burned-out due to overcommitment, while the Family-committed exit the profession in search of a better work–life balance. Finally, the Marginalized are pushed out of journalism by structural or organizational pressures. The typology reveals that leaving the profession is often perceived as an involuntary process, underscoring the need for media organizations to implement strategies aimed at keeping journalists in the field.

latest.title: Intrapreneurial Practices in News Media Organisations: A Multi-level Analysis
latest.abstract: News media organisations are under constant pressure to innovate and renew themselves. Under these conditions, intrapreneurship offers a way to advance innovation from within existing organisations by enabling employees to initiate, develop, and promote new ideas as part of their everyday work. This article examines how intrapreneurial practices support innovation in journalism and media work. Drawing on a practice-based, multi-level framework, the study analyses intrapreneurial activity at individual, team, and organisational levels in two Finnish news media companies. Based on a dual-case study of semi-structured interviews with media managers, the analysis examines concrete episodes that explain how intrapreneurial activity is initiated, advanced, and supported in journalism and media work. The findings show how intrapreneurial activity is enacted through interconnected practices across levels and depends on surrounding organisational conditions. The article offers a systematic way to analyse intrapreneurial activity in journalism and offers practical insights for news media professionals and organisations seeking renewal by showing how innovation is put into practice in everyday media work.

latest.title: Publishers’ Power: The Influence of Ownership on the Framing of Dutch Media Concentration (2003–2022)
latest.abstract: Journalism operates in market-based systems, forcing news outlets to balance editorial autonomy with financial imperatives. This friction raises concerns about media owners’ influence on news content, particularly coverage directly tied to their financial interests, such as media mergers. To examine this influence, we conducted an inductive-then-deductive content analysis on news coverage of media mergers, assessing which justifying and criticizing frames appeared and whether their use differed when the outlet’s owner was involved in the merger. The analysis focused on the period between 2003 and 2022 in the Netherlands, where strong editorial safeguards coexist with high media concentration. Findings showed that reporting on media mergers focused primarily on who owns the media and why, rather than on broader implications for the news market. Outlets used significantly more justifying frames when covering mergers involving their owner compared to when the owner was not involved. No difference was found for criticizing frames. Furthermore, while the Dutch market became increasingly concentrated, recent mergers featured more justifying but not fewer criticizing frames. Similarly, outlets undergoing takeovers engaged in more justification, while criticism was unaffected. Overall, the results call for a reconsideration of the presumed resilience of journalistic autonomy against corporate pressures in democratic markets.

latest.title: Pressured by the Comments? Chinese Journalists in the Face of Online Violence
latest.abstract: In the increasingly digital context of China’s public sphere, journalists frequently encounter online violence that threatens their professional autonomy, emotional wellbeing, and freedom of expression. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with journalists representing a cross section of the Chinese media landscape, this study identifies four major types of online violence experienced by Chinese journalists: violence in response to alleged unprofessional behaviours, violence based on moral coercion, violence motivated by so-called “nationalism”, and gendered violence. Cultural norms, nationalist ideologies, and patriarchy emerge as key factors shaping and underpinning online violence. With regard to journalists’ coping strategies, these are found to include individualised and emotionally taxing approaches, such as silence, avoidance and contempt, while institutional support is either limited in its responsiveness or sometimes unavailable. This study provides an enhanced understanding of the role of online violence in shaping journalistic practice and coping strategies in a highly interactive and emotional digital media environment. The findings indicate that online violence driven by wider structural and cultural forces, is becoming an increasingly common informal control mechanism, undermining journalistic authority and autonomy and therefore the stability and sustainability of journalism itself.

latest.title: News is Becoming Similar? A Diachronic Text Mining Exploration of News Convergence in Chinese Media
latest.abstract: The convergence of news has long been a central concern in media studies, yet empirical evidence and precise measurements remain limited. China’s unique media system, which operates simultaneously in domestic and global contexts under distinct communication strategies, offers a rare opportunity to advance this line of inquiry. This study draws on news posts (N = 607,871) from four leading Chinese outlets over the past decade and applies a text-mining approach to examine Chinese news convergence across the two contexts and its relationship with audience news engagement. The results show a significant increase in lexical similarity among Chinese media in the global context but not in the domestic context. No upward trend in thematic structural similarity is observed in either context. Moreover, the associations between convergence and audience engagement are context-dependent: in the domestic context, lexical similarity is negatively associated with engagement, whereas in the global context, both lexical and thematic similarity are positively associated with engagement. These results challenge conventional views of news convergence, highlighting its dynamic nature across temporal and contextual dimensions. Further implications for theory and practice are discussed.

latest.title: Satire in Exile: Exiled Newsfluencers' use of Satire as a Discursive Strategy
latest.abstract: This article examines how one newsfluencer in exile employs satire as a discursive strategy to sustain counter-publics in autocratic contexts. Through a multimodal critical discourse analysis of twenty videos by Stephen Shiu, a prominent Hong Kong newsfluencer now based in Taiwan, this article identifies a range of satirical strategies used in his commentary, including irony, exaggeration, parody, mock expertise, profanity, insult, metaphor, rumour, and personal anecdote. Drawing from these findings, we discuss how, in this case, satirists in exile may help provide critical information when domestic journalism is silenced, articulate collective frustration through emotional expression, and preserve local Cantonese profanity as a form of identity politics. This article adds to the literature on satire and social media by showing that online platforms like YouTube provide newsfluencers in exile with greater freedom of expression than would have been possible in legacy media, as well as sustain critical journalism in exile.

latest.title: Future Problems, Present Challenges: Exploring Journalistic Practices and the Normative Role of Journalism in Reporting Persistent Social Issues
latest.abstract: Persistent social issues shaping our collective future, such as climate change and aging populations, are among the most pressing challenges facing society. They are inherently complex, and their long-term, uncertain, and global nature clashes with journalistic preferences for proximity, immediacy, and audience relevance. This raises questions about how persistent social issues are handled in day-to-day journalism. Drawing on 15 in-depth interviews, this study explores how Dutch journalists navigate reporting on persistent social issues. Findings show that some journalistic selection and framing considerations are business-as-usual. However, these issues complicate considerations around maintaining salience and upholding journalistic values. Journalists articulate that the distant, complex, and persistent issue characteristics conflict with media logic, resulting in specific navigation strategies, such as bridging psychological distance and integrating multiple perspectives. Beyond selection and presentation considerations, journalists conceptualize two normative role understandings: journalism as communicator of complexity and facilitator of public engagement. These roles are difficult to reconcile, as strategies that foster engagement risk oversimplification, while conveying complexity risks disengagement. The study contributes by identifying tensions journalists navigate across structurally similar issues from diverse domains, advancing debates on journalistic responsibility, and offering insights into supporting sustained coverage that counters societal short-termism.

latest.title: “If No One Is Doing Anything, What’s the Point of Hearing about It Again and Again?” Youth, Climate Journalism and Mediated Public (Dis)connection
latest.abstract: For news media, climate journalism has been identified as both a normative responsibility and a strategic beat for reaching young audiences. This paper examines whether and how news media shape engagement with and public connection to climate change among Norwegian youth. Drawing on an in-depth qualitative study of 33 participants in a high-choice, digitally advanced media environment, I analyse the place of climate journalism in everyday media repertoires of youth. Prior engagement is decisive: climate issues are salient for already-concerned youth, but largely absent among others. Across groups, news media are not primary sources for climate information or engagement, suggesting that news-centric audience research may overstate news media’s role in public engagement with climate change and overlook youth-specific media habits. Combining different mediated public connection frameworks, the study shows why news media often fail to connect young people to climate change as a public issue. It introduces two interrelated analytical concepts: a lack of spatiotemporally grounded solutions in news coverage, which can lead to informed disconnection, a form of public disconnection with climate change partly produced by, rather than resolved by, climate journalism. Further, it proposes practice-oriented recommendations.

latest.title: Survival Tactics: Investigative Journalism Methods Under Threats and Barriers in Kazakhstan
latest.abstract: Investigative journalists face growing legal, physical, psychological, and institutional pressures that shape how investigations are conducted. While prior research has documented risks to journalists, little empirical work has examined how different threats reconfigure investigative methods, particularly in Kazakhstan. This study addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 13 investigative journalists. The findings show that risk does not lead to the abandonment of investigative practices but to method-specific adaptations. Legal threats encourage the use of legally defensible approaches such as open-source research, official documents, data journalism, and collaboration, while discouraging anonymous sources and undercover work. Physical threats shift investigations toward remote and digitally mediated practices. Psychological pressure favors emotionally sustainable, analytical methods, and structural barriers limit access to official information, prompting reliance on independent data reconstruction and verification. By linking specific threats to distinct methodological responses, the study offers an empirically grounded framework for understanding how risk reshapes investigative journalism in Kazakhstan.

latest.title: Facebook Community Standards: The New Gatekeeper for Palestinian News Organizations?
latest.abstract: This study examines how Facebook’s Community Standards act as a “gatekeeper” in ways that shape the editorial practices of Palestinian news organizations. It investigates how Facebook’s policies and algorithms influence their coverage of Palestine and the Israeli occupation. Findings reveal that these organizations navigate platform censorship by altering content and turning to platforms like Telegram to avoid restrictions, highlighting the tension between freedom of speech and maintaining visibility under digital constraints.

latest.title: Under Construction: Democracy Reporting as Paradigm Repair
latest.abstract: In recent years, several news organizations in the United States have added a new beat to their newsrooms: the democracy beat. In this study, we analyze the metajournalistic discourse about the creation of teams tasked with democracy-specific reporting. We contribute to scholarship about the relationship between democracy and journalism at a time when both are under duress. The creation of democracy beats, we find, is a critique of political reporting as usual and an exercise in both paradigm repair and paradigm renewal. News outlets are trying to rehabilitate the normative role of journalists as watchdogs and defenders of democracy. Democracy desks are expected to adopt a more adversarial approach and critical standpoint as they challenge the objectivity paradigm. This study provides valuable insights into the institutional response of U.S. news organizations at the local, state, and national levels to attacks on the free press and to the escalating anti-media rhetoric putting journalism’s institutional role in a democratic society to the test.

latest.title: Growing Inequalities Through Motivations: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Between Socioeconomic Status, Political Interest and News Media Consumption in Sweden, 1990–2023
latest.abstract: As we have transitioned toward media systems increasingly characterized by proliferation of media choices, public and scholarly concern regarding widening news consumption gaps have grown. Two types of gaps have been especially prominent in research on news audience fragmentation. The first is research building on the opportunity, motivation and abilities (OMA) framework, showing that individual motivations and preferences are becoming more important when it comes to news consumption. The second is research focused on how high-choice media environments might contribute to socioeconomic (SES) gaps in news consumption. We know from previous research that these two gaps are related since SES shapes political interest through socialization processes, which in turn drives news consumption. However, previous research lacks an integrated longitudinal perspective, testing whether this mediated relationship has increased over time. Addressing these shortcomings, we utilize 33 years of Swedish survey data (NRespondents = 47 884) to conduct a moderated mediation analysis, simultaneously studying the direct effect of socioeconomic status as well as its indirect – mediated through political interest – effect on news consumption. Results suggest that socioeconomic gaps in news consumption have grown and that an important driver of these differences might be due to an increasing indirect effect through political interest.

latest.title: The Somatechnic Hermeneutic: “Embodying” the Worlds of Journalism Study
latest.abstract: This study introduces a somatechnic hermeneutic to bridge the theoretical insights of the bodily turn in journalism studies with the empirical architecture of large-scale survey research, exemplified by the Worlds of Journalism Study (WJS). We argue that indicators such as safety, autonomy, precarity, and role conceptions are not merely abstract variables but proxies for lived, embodied experience. Applying this hermeneutic to Portugal's paradoxical profile–marked by high physical safety alongside acute economic precarity–we identify a state of somatic dissonance, in which the journalistic body is caught between physical protection and systemic strain. Through comparative analysis, we demonstrate how this dissonance fractures professional self-perception, revealing that professional role commitments are not only cognitive ideals but also corporeal practices. This approach re-frames perceptual survey data into a narrative of embodied experience and provides a framework for addressing empirical paradoxes, offering a transferable methodology for understanding how the pressures of journalism are somatically registered and endured across diverse media systems.

latest.title: Journalists in a Multicrisis Situation: External Crises as Accelerators of Long-Term Internal Crises and a Lost Opportunity for Resilience Building
latest.abstract: Recent crises epitomise the current age of disruption within journalism. Journalism faces a multicrisis situation, where internal issues—mainly economic and technological—accumulate with external predicaments, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, or the war in Ukraine, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. From the perspective of resilience building, such disruptions may represent not only threats but also opportunities for change and adaptation. To explore journalists’ interpretations of the relationship between their occupation and large societal crises, we conducted in-depth interviews to show how journalists perceive the disruptions of their work and how they build their professional resilience, focusing on a specific context of a post-transformation Central European country, the Czech Republic. Our findings suggest that large external crises are perceived as accelerators for long-term internal crises in the profession, which, due to the lack of deep collective reflection, represent a wasted opportunity for systemic change. Instead, they push professionals into individualised solutions and highlight the conflict between their social responsibility and the economic pressures of competitiveness.

trending.title: Knowledge Silos as a Barrier to Responsible AI Practices in Journalism? Exploratory Evidence from Four Dutch News Organisations
trending.abstract: The effective adoption of responsible AI practices in journalism requires a concerted effort to bridge different perspectives, including technological, editorial, and managerial. Among the many challenges that could impact information sharing around responsible AI inside news organisations are knowledge silos, where information is isolated within one part of the organisation and not easily shared with others. This study aims to study how knowledge silos might affect the adoption of responsible AI practices in journalism through a cross-case study of four Dutch media outlets. We examine individual and organisational barriers to AI knowledge sharing and the extent to which knowledge silos could impede the operationalisation of responsible AI initiatives inside these newsrooms. To address this question, we conducted 14 semi-structured interviews with a strategic sample of editors, managers, and journalists at de Telegraaf, de Volkskrant, NOS, and RTL Nederland. The interviews aimed to uncover insights into the existence of knowledge silos, their effects on responsible AI practice adoption, and the organisational practices influencing these dynamics. Our results emphasise the importance of creating better structures for sharing information on AI across all layers of news organisations and highlight the need for research on knowledge silos as an impediment to responsible AI production.

trending.title: AI in the Newsroom: Does the Public Trust Automated Journalism and Will They Pay for It?
trending.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adapted for news production tasks in news outlets worldwide. Whether the public trusts news outlets relying on AI to produce news remains unclear. Further, the economic implications (willingness to pay and ad acceptance) and moderators remain unexplored. We conducted a pre-registered 2 × 2 experiment with a quota-based nonprobability sample from Germany (N = 1,261). Respondents were exposed to vignettes about a fictional online news outlet. We manipulated the production process (generative AI vs. trained journalists, between-subject) and the topic covered (politics vs. entertainment, within-subject). Participants trusted outlets with AI-generated news less, particularly political ones. They were less willing to accept seeing ads shown by AI outlets and outlets that covered entertainment. Willingness to pay was not affected. We explored moderators: Individuals with the perception that AIs spread incorrect information were less trusting in AI-generated news. These perceptions did not moderate the relationship with willingness to pay or ad acceptance. The opinion climate did not moderate the effect of the content production process. In sum, AI in the newsroom may decrease trust and ad revenue of outlets. This effect might be exacerbated depending on audience characteristics. We discuss implications for theory, future scholarship, and media organizations.

trending.title: Fact-Checking in Journalism: An Epistemological Framework
trending.abstract: Fact-checking has become an enduring form of journalism that can influence public discussion and counter false content on mass media and social media platforms. However, communication scholars have questioned some epistemological premises of fact-checking and their embeddedness in journalistic practices. This study examines the validity of this criticism by defining three deep-rooted challenges threatening to compromise the epistemological basis of fact-checking. We analysed the problems related to degrees of objectivism, truth regimes, and causal relations across five different aspects of fact-checking to trace where epistemological concerns originate and how they can be resolved. Consequently, we provide a set of measures (rigour, presentation, and audience engagement) that can be used to explore the nature of epistemological problems in fact-checking contexts. We argue that these measures can support and reinforce the epistemological foundations of fact-checking if they are applied in a way that transparently recognises the subjective elements included in fact-checking work. Recognition of subjective elements is essential when developing novel and existing fact-checking methods, given the risks of bias replication and subjectivity in AI-powered systems and other technological solutions.

trending.title: News on TikTok Through the Lens of Quality Journalism: How TikTok Users Perceive News Values, Content, and Engagement
trending.abstract: As TikTok becomes an increasingly popular platform for news consumption, it is important to understand how its unique format aligns with or challenges traditional journalistic standards. This study draws on the quality journalism framework, which consists of professional norms, content features, and audience engagement dimensions, to examine how U.S. TikTok users perceive the quality of news they encounter on the platform. Based on in-depth interviews with 23 TikTok news users, we find that while entertainment is a main motivation for using TikTok, users still value traditional journalistic principles such as information utility, accuracy, and credibility. Users express different expectations for news quality depending on the news topic and the source, whether the content comes from influencers or legacy media. Many users view TikTok news as an entry point to learning about current events and often seek out additional information on other platforms. Our findings suggest that users expect TikTok journalism to maintain a balance between engaging presentation and journalistic rigor. This study contributes to the growing literature on TikTok journalism by focusing on audience perspectives and offering a nuanced look at how news quality is understood within the TikTok context.

trending.title: On Controlled Change: Generative AI’s Impact on Professional Authority in Journalism
trending.abstract: Using (generative) artificial intelligence tools and systems in journalism is expected to increase journalists’ production rates, transform newsrooms’ economic models, and further personalize the audience’s news consumption practices. Since its release in 2022, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and other large language models have raised alarms within news organizations, not only for introducing new challenges to news reporting and fact-checking but also for what these technologies would mean for journalists’ professional authority. This paper examines how journalists in Dutch media integrate AI technologies into their daily routines. Drawing on 13 interviews with editors, journalists, and innovation managers across different news outlets and media companies, we use controlled change as an interpretative frame derived from empirical data to explain how journalists are proactively setting guidelines, experimenting with AI tools, and identifying their limitations and capabilities. Using professional authority as a theoretical framework, we argue that journalists anticipate and integrate AI technologies in a supervised manner and identify three primary mechanisms through which journalists manage this integration: (1) developing adaptive guidelines that align AI use with ethical codes, (2) experimenting with AI technologies to determine their necessity and fit, and (3) critically assessing the capabilities and limitations of AI systems.

trending.title: An Experiential View of What Short Digital News Practices Mean from An Audience Perspective
trending.abstract: This paper explores short digital news practices from an audience perspective. Following declining revenues and an increased focus on audiences, the metric of time spent has become a key parameter for measuring people’s attention and engagement with news. With people spending less time, concerns have accordingly been raised about the future of journalism and the quality of people’s informedness. By focusing on how audiences experience and navigate news online, this paper problematizes longstanding assumptions about the relationship between time spent and interest in news. Drawing on empirical data from two interview rounds with Norwegian news users, combined with video-ethnography, media diaries, and data donations, the study contributes to existing research on time spent (and lost) on news by untangling the temporal experiences and practices of news audiences. Findings show short and dispersed consumption patterns to be (1) parts of overall cross-media news practices; (2) expressions of skilled navigation; (3) expressions of reassurance and control; and (4) automated and unintended practices.

trending.title: Journalism and Embodied Knowledge: Conceptualizing Affective Epistemology and Epistemic Affordances of Emotions and Affect Across News Beats
trending.abstract: This conceptual paper aims to theorize the role of journalists’ bodies in knowledge-making practices by focusing on affects and emotions as a mediatrix of biological, social, and political bodies. It does so by developing the concepts of journalists’ “affective epistemology” and “epistemic affordances” of emotions and affect that, altogether, aim to provide journalism researchers with a conceptual toolkit for studying the role of emotions and affect in journalistic epistemology. The notion of affective epistemology is based on (1) relevant empirical research on journalism, emotions, and affect, (2) Feminist Standpoint Epistemology, and (3) selected philosophical, sociological, and anthropological theories of emotions and embodied knowledge. The paper also identifies five epistemic affordances of emotions and affect in journalism, i.e., ways how they can be illuminating as well as blinding in journalists’ knowledge-building and fact-finding practices: motivational, methodological-analytical, ontological-narrative, collaborative-innovative, and phatic-interactional. Examples illustrating these affordances come from existing research on various journalism beats, from lifestyle and cultural journalism to conflict reporting. In conclusion, I ask how journalists can integrate emotions in knowledge-building practices in a way that makes emotions rather illuminating than blinding. I suggest that a productive use of emotions/affects requires maximum reflexivity, virtue responsibility, and emotional literacy.

trending.title: AI in Media Consumption: Charting the Futures of Journalism
trending.abstract: The use of generative AI in media consumption has the potential to significantly reshape the media environment and the relationship between journalism and its audience. However, as research on the potential of AI and algorithms for media and journalism has largely focused on newsroom applications, the implications of potentially increasing audience uses largely remain unexplored. We examine this potential shift from the perspective of journalistic media, using a design fiction methodology to explore scenarios of future media consumption enabled by generative AI technologies. Through a study involving media professionals from diverse backgrounds, we identify four possible trajectories for journalism: its marginalization, its resilience through human connection, its persistence as a key source of information, and its adaptation through AI-enhanced tools and technological advancements. Based on our results, we consider key decision points for media institutions that may shape which of these futures ultimately unfold.

trending.title: Bringing Up the Body: Uncovering the Subjectivity of Journalists
trending.abstract: In this paper, I discuss major contributions to journalism studies that come from approaching journalistic practice from the vantage point of the body – that is, understanding how journalists go about their work in ways shaped by their embodied experience. I will develop the argument that a consideration of the journalistic body requires a challenge to the fundamental underpinnings of professional practice, which are premised on the invisibility of the body. Foregrounding the body in relation to journalism practice calls for greater reflexivity in relation to the subjectivity of journalists. The paper discusses three overlapping insights resulting from such an approach: First, it requires attention to individual journalists’ bodies and lived experience in relation to their pasts – or what journalists “carry.” Second, it calls for attention to how they feel in the present – and how these affective responses shape their practice. Finally, it requires charting how journalists’ bodies interact with other bodies, and the institutions surrounding them, as they go about their work.

trending.title: Deepfakes and Journalism: Normative Considerations and Implications
trending.abstract: The possibility of using deepfake technology to create synthetic media content in journalism requires careful ethical deliberations. Being that journalism is a norm-oriented social institution, there should be a commitment to ethical principles, which raises questions about the compatibility of this technology’s application with journalistic norms. There is a lack of knowledge on how these challenges can be addressed. This research presents four lenses on the compatibility of deepfakes with journalism, which emerged from a qualitative study involving 26 journalists. First, the understanding of deepfakes shapes how their use is evaluated. Second, judgments depend on what is manipulated in the deepfake and to what extent. Third, journalists need to carefully consider the connection between deepfakes and reality. Finally, specific normative preconditions must be met for the application of deepfakes in journalism. This study argues that the compatibility of deepfake technology with journalistic ethics varies, depending on whether it is used to create or manipulate (1) the presentation, (2) the content, or (3) the subject of the content or the event itself. Although there are numerous possibilities to integrate deepfake technology in journalism, it is imperative that journalism remains resilient in upholding its fundamental norms and ethical standards.

trending.title: Thriving in Journalism: A Survey of Support Systems’ Impact on Job Satisfaction and Well-Being
trending.abstract: Journalists rely on a patchwork of support from organizational, institutional, and interpersonal sources, about which the academic literature has growing evidence. Building on this literature, this study seeks to provide such an overview, while also asking how well these patchwork supports function. A nationally representative survey of 633 U.S. reporters finds that trust in management and a supportive workplace culture are most important for journalists’ job satisfaction; work–life balance and support from family and friends are most important for journalists’ overall well-being. Income was a strong predictor of both job satisfaction and well-being. Overall, results point to the important role of editors as creators of workplace culture and front-line caregivers, suggesting a need for management training.

trending.title: Decoding Correction Strategies: How Fact-Checkers Uncover Falsehoods Across Countries
trending.abstract: This study systematically analyzes and compares verification strategies employed by fact-checking organizations across various contexts. Utilizing a dataset of 3,154 verification articles from 23 organizations in eight countries across Europe and Latin America, the study identifies 17 distinct debunking techniques through both inductive and deductive approaches. The primary objectives are to uncover common and divergent practices in factual correction, assess how techniques vary by verification target (e.g., online rumors versus statements by public figures), and examine variations at organizational and national levels. The findings reveal that while methods such as providing documents and tracing misinformation origins are prevalent, significant variation exists depending on the target. For online rumors, common practices include tracing misinformation origins, forensic analysis, and visual indicators of image manipulation. Conversely, verification of public figure statements frequently involves expert arbitration and direct contact with misinformation sources. Additionally, the study highlights substantial differences in fact-checking strategies across countries and organizations, influenced by their focus and institutional contexts. This research addresses a notable gap in the literature by offering a comparative analysis of verification strategies, providing a framework for future experimental research, and offering guidance for fact-checkers and scholars to refine their approaches to combating misinformation.

trending.title: Whose Voices Shape Protest Narratives? Comparing Source Diversity in Kenya’s Digital-Native and Legacy-Affiliated News Coverage
trending.abstract: This study investigates the construction of protest narratives in online-only and legacy-affiliated digital news media, specifically examining their sourcing practices during Kenya’s 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests. By analyzing the digital-native outlet Kenyans.co.ke alongside the legacy outlet Citizen Digital, the research reveals significant yet subtle differences in source diversity. Both platforms primarily depend on authoritative voices, with government officials making up 32% of sources in each outlet. However, Kenyans.co.ke provides slightly more representation for protesters and activists (27.7% vs. 23.9%) and the general public (16.9% vs. 14.9%), along with a greater reliance on social media sources (9.2% vs. 7.5%). These findings indicate that digital-native platforms may afford a somewhat wider array of grassroots perspectives, though neither outlet substantially diverges from the dominance of official sources. This study highlights a critical tension in protest coverage: while digital platforms open avenues for diverse voices, institutional narratives continue to prevail. By examining these continuities and disruptions, the research enriches discussions about media democratization, the limitations of journalistic practices, and the potential for alternative sourcing to transform protest narratives. It calls for a deeper examination of how both legacy and digital media architectures either reinforce or challenge existing power dynamics in public discourse.

trending.title: Broadcasting through the (New) Iron Curtain: Practices, Challenges, and Legacies of Russia's Independent Media in Exile
trending.abstract: The Russo-Ukrainian war and the Kremlin's military censorship have made independent reporting from within Russia impossible. After a few weeks of the conflict, all institutional journalism was forced into exile. Funding sources, access to informants, and the ability to provide objective conflict coverage quickly vanished. Now in exile, Russian journalists have become entirely reliant on donor funding to sustain operations and on new technologies to reach audiences inside Russia. Over 18 months in exile, we conducted more than 50 interviews with editors-in-chief, senior correspondents, and individual journalists adapting to these new circumstances. We asked about audience access, funding opportunities, reliance on new technologies, and organisational challenges within newsrooms. This paper argues that these new conditions have underscored pre-existing issues within Russian media while introducing challenges brought about by the war and exile. However, in a global context, these issues closely mirror those faced by exiled journalists worldwide.

trending.title: “I Feel It in My Body, in My Soul, in My Mind”: Journalism, Racist News and Immigrants’ Experience of Belonging
trending.abstract: We know that journalism, and particularly news, has an essential function in society and politics and that it shapes our understanding of reality. Yet, we fail to recognize its far-reaching implications on the lived experience of those who consume it. This article contributes towards addressing this gap by examining the response of individuals with an immigrant background to racist representations of immigrants in Norwegian news during the Covid-19 pandemic. It involved 21 in-depth interviews that mapped how the coverage both was entwined with and refracted through the participants’ emotions, embodied and situated experiences, impacting their sense of belonging in Norwegian society. The analysis demonstrates the devastating reverberations of racist news discourse on all domains of an immigrant’s life: far from merely providing information, news profoundly affects an immigrant’s sense of safety, health and well-being, and feeling (or not) “at home.” The study has relevance beyond the Norwegian case and the timeframe of the pandemic in so far as it moves beyond existing research about “news effects” and “audience studies.” Theoretically it conceptualizes news as both elemental and existential. Methodologically, it approaches it as woven into the experience of immigrants rather than as an external influence on it.

trending.title: Activists for Diversity or Diverse Journalists? How Austrian Peripheral Journalistic Actors’ Role Orientations Serve as Boundary Markers
trending.abstract: Technological innovations have signaled a shift in the journalistic field, enabling a wider range of actors to participate in public discourses and challenge the hegemonic power structures of traditional journalism from the outside. Consequently, historical notions of alternative media have expanded to encompass a variety of new actors within and beyond the boundaries of the journalistic field, with some explicitly claiming to focus on issues of diversity. This study examines the role orientations of peripheral journalistic actors who prioritize journalistic diversity in their work. It also explores how they use their role orientations to position themselves within the journalistic field and its periphery. Based on 18 in-depth interviews with Austrian peripheral actors, the study finds that while their role orientations diverge from those of more traditional media, they share similarities with longstanding normative ideas of progressive alternative media. Further, they employ their cognitive and normative role orientations as boundary markers to distinguish themselves from the practices of more traditional media.

trending.title: Bodily Realities in Digital Journalism: The Role of User-Generated Content in Embodied Witnessing
trending.abstract: In the evolving digital era, user-generated content (UGC) plays a crucial role in shaping journalistic narratives, shedding light on the corporeal realities of news coverage. This study delves into the embodied nature of UGC—its visual, auditory, and emotional components—that significantly enhance the perceptual immediacy and authenticity of news. Utilizing descriptive and correlational analyses, this research examines how these embodied characteristics impact journalistic authenticity and emotional resonance. The findings illuminate that aspects such as on-site Filming and emotional Language are closely linked with journalistic objectivity and emotional intensity. Moreover, the incorporation of UGC foregrounds ethical challenges, highlighting concerns over privacy and misinformation, which are pivotal in maintaining journalistic integrity. This analysis underscores the necessity for news organizations to adeptly navigate these complexities, promoting an understanding of how the corporeal engagement facilitated by UGC redefines journalistic practices and values. By emphasizing the material and discursive positioning of bodies in journalism, this paper contributes to broader discussions on the corporeal dimensions of communication in the digital age, offering guidelines for establishing ethical standards that respect both the integrity of news and its inherently participatory nature.

trending.title: Navigating Platform Dependency: Four Strategic Approaches for Social Media News Publishing
trending.abstract: This article examines how Norwegian newsrooms attempt to secure editorial autonomy while engaging with social media platforms. Drawing on qualitative interviews with 16 newsroom actors and two weeks of field observation, it explores how editorial strategies are enacted through everyday practices. Using a strategy-as-practice perspective, we identify four approaches to social media publishing – the Negotiator, the Preserver, the Adapter, and the Withdrawer – each reflecting different combinations of strategic coherence, resources, and editorial priorities. Building on the distinction between “independence from” and “independence to”, the study shows that autonomy is not fixed but continuously negotiated between professional ideals and platform constraints. While resources largely determine outlets’ ability to resist platform interference (independence from), deliberate strategic engagement can strengthen journalism’s capacity to reach and inform publics (independence to). The paper contributes to the ongoing debates on journalism's platform dependency by highlighting the importance of editors’ and journalists’ strategic agency in everyday work.

trending.title: ChatBots as Artificial Intermediaries? Adaptation to Artificial Intelligence in Newsrooms
trending.abstract: Journalists have long claimed authority regarding the distribution of valid knowledge and hence, have discursively placed themselves in an intermediary role between audiences and the information they seek. Threats to this authority are not new, yet the threats posed by generative artificial intelligence offer a novel presentation of this threat: could the distribution of valid knowledge be replicated by chatbots? This study explores the discursive construction of artificial intelligence in four countries (Canada, Germany, UK, USA) through a dataset of metajournalism articles (n = 177) produced in the early stages of ChatGPT 3.5. We find that journalists perceived potential and addressable pitfalls in working with artificial intelligence but worried less about the implications for their audiences.

trending.title: Visual Politics, Protest, and Power: Who Shaped the Climate Visual Discourse at COP26?
trending.abstract: Despite the importance of visual imagery for how people conceptualise issues in the news media, most research on journalism and communication prioritises textual media. This research examines the visual imagery accompanying news stories about the 2021 UN Climate Summit in Glasgow (COP26). Using a mixed-methods approach, we analyse over 1,300 images from eight UK news outlets using content and critical visual discourse analysis. We then contextualise these images, drawing on interviews and participant observation with key visual media actors including image agency photojournalists and news journalists, editors and correspondents. First, we find that the visual discourse of COP26 is limited to politicians and “talking heads” imagery, and images of protest. Second, we explore the journey that images take through the news media ecosystem, from the camera lens to the published news article, identifying the sources of power which act on visuals throughout this journey. Sources of power can be obvious (e.g., individual photographers), whilst others are obscured or misattributed (e.g., curation and editing). Overall, we empirically demonstrate the importance of understanding the networked nature of images and how they move through a complex globalised media ecosystem, rather than conceptualising them simply as static objects in the news cycle.

trending.title: Is Press Freedom Better Protected in Democracies? Internet Shutdown and Journalism in India
trending.abstract: It's commonly assumed that democracies are comparatively better than non-democratic regimes in safeguarding press freedom from political interference and ensuring constitutional and regulatory safeguards. Although this perception is largely true, numerous recent examples have shown journalism coming under attack in democratic regimes too. Drawing upon qualitative interviews conducted with journalists during and after the world's longest internet shutdown in the state of Jammu and Kashmir in India in 2019, this article underscores the measures used by the Indian government to control the flow of information. The article unpacks the dynamics of reporting by local, national and international media during the internet shutdown and shows how differing perceptions of their roles allowed journalists to perform their professional tasks even in difficult situations. Given the fact that repression of journalistic freedom occurred in a democracy, and at a time when the world is more connected than before, this not only challenges the normative understanding of how journalism functions in democracies but it may also hold lessons for journalists in circumventing the use of such tactics in other democracies.

trending.title: True Crime Podcasting as Journalistic Heterodoxy: Boundary Practices and Journalistic Epistemology of a Heretic Interloper
trending.abstract: Non-fictional true crime reporting has enjoyed a somewhat deviant position within the journalistic field and has been rejected as sensationalist and not considered “good” journalism by journalistic discourse. Relative to other peripheral forms of journalism, podcasting has received comparatively less attention even as the medium is considered the fastest growing. Through the lens of boundary work, this study investigates six US true crime podcasts to explore their epistemic practices and how they approach ethical dilemmas in reporting. This study argues that podcasts display a largely subjective approach to truthmaking, embracing the entertaining power of stories to create change. Most podcast series studied employ longstanding sourcing and reporting practices to legitimize their position within the journalistic field, reflecting the transferable values of journalism to new forms of reporting.

trending.title: What “Digital Literacies” Must Journalists Have? Unpacking How Journalists Define and Practice News Literacy, Data Literacy, and Algorithmic and AI Literacy in the Digital Age
trending.abstract: As media environments become increasingly complex, with a myriad of actors producing news, new technologies entering into newsrooms, and a large amount of data and (fake) news in circulation, journalists must obtain a set of “digital literacies” essential to function in the newsroom. Such literacies will enable journalists to perform their public service role to accurately inform the citizenry; currently, journalist perspectives on this topic have never been explored. Through in-depth interviews with journalists and editors, this study reveals “news literacy”, “data literacy”, “algorithmic literacy” and “AI literacy” as core to contemporary journalistic work—participants in this study offered their own definitions of these terms, and how these literacies are put into practice as actual newsroom behaviors, such as research, verification, diversification of sources, contextualization of data, and search engine optimization. Given obstacles such as time constraints, unfamiliarity with new technologies, and the presence of certain beliefs and discourses that might hinder the practice of such literacies, this paper points to two factors that can encourage such literacy behaviors—pertaining to (1) personal motivations and (2) organizational norms and structures—to increase journalistic knowledge and skills in the digital age.

trending.title: Navigating Connections and Disconnections: The (Re)making of Russian Exiled Journalism in the Digital Age
trending.abstract: The growing shift of many countries toward authoritarianism has led to an increase in exiled media communities. This study examines the dual identity of exiled journalists: as new immigrants who must adapt to their host countries, and as media professionals who must maintain ties with their estranged homeland. Drawing on extensive empirical data from interviews with Russian exiled journalists and fieldwork done in 2023, it develops an analytical approach to understanding exiled media as a constellation of connections to, and disconnections from, both home and host spaces. On the one hand, Russian exiled journalists strive to navigate and reproduce a digitised reality of the home country, transcending the physical boundaries and restrictions imposed by nation-states. On the other, their lack of physical presence in Russia fosters a fear of losing their intimate understanding of the homeland and, consequently, their professional authority. Paradoxically, their efforts to stay connected to Russia and keep journalistic doxa deepen their disconnection from their host country and hinder their personal and professional integration. As such, their occupation, “Russian journalist”, becomes a symbolic shelter to maintain the professional status quo. To mitigate isolation in the host society, journalists cultivate alternative connections with exiled journalists from other countries.

trending.title: Beyond Audience Evaluations: Re-Thinking News Trust in Digital Environments
trending.abstract: This paper re-examines the concept of news trust within the context of the current media environment. Commonly defined as audiences’ willingness to be vulnerable to media objects, news trust has occupied scholars for almost a century and has gained heightened attention due to public concerns over misinformation. However, certain limitations continue to challenge its theoretical and empirical conceptualization. Drawing upon an integrative review of the current state of the field, I offer a comprehensive conceptual framework of news trust within contemporary media ecosystems. This framework extends existing theorizations by incorporating the journalistic, prospective, and emotional dimensions of news trust. In doing so it extends the audience-centered perspective that dominates existing literature; adjusts the research on news trust to the recent emphasis on emotions in political communication and journalism studies; and bridges theoretical frameworks of trust from sociology, psychology, and communication.
